chapters.label: THE VIEW
chapters.title: This is a gorge stop, not a riverbank stop
chapters.body: The Champi and Pak Koot streams fall side by side into a deep forested gorge. That separation is what gives Tad Fane its shape. The essential visit is simple: stand back, read the two drops together and let the depth do the work. Rainy-season flow is stronger, but mist and cloud can also soften or briefly hide the view.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Tad Fane earns its place through scale. If you want a waterfall you can explore more closely, make Tad Yuang the complementary stop.

items.label: Format
items.detail: The classic experience is from the gorge side rather than a long walk beside the river.

items.label: From Paksé
items.detail: Use Tad Fane as one anchor in a Bolaven Plateau half day or full day instead of driving out for a single photograph.

items.label: Conditions & entry
items.detail: Rainy-season flow is strongest, while drier conditions can give cleaner visibility. Confirm current entrance and parking fees locally.

faq.question: What is special about Tad Fane?
faq.answer: Two streams plunge roughly 120 metres side by side into a deep rainforest gorge. The attraction is the scale and twin-drop composition rather than a close-up swimming stop.

faq.question: How long do I need at Tad Fane?
faq.answer: Around 45 to 90 minutes is enough for the main viewpoint experience. Allow a half day once the road from Paksé and another plateau stop are included.

faq.question: Is Tad Fane better than Tad Yuang?
faq.answer: They do different jobs. Tad Fane is the stronger wide gorge view; Tad Yuang is the better choice if you want paths and several closer viewpoints around a waterfall.

faq.question: When is Tad Fane most impressive?
faq.answer: Rainy-season flow is the most powerful. For a clearer view into the gorge, drier conditions can be easier, so choose between water volume and visibility rather than expecting both every day.
